abstract: Unexpected visual events can leave goal pursuit undisturbed or trigger visual action override - an interruption that redirects behaviour towards the stimulus. Using a visual distraction task in freely moving mice, population calcium recordings and causal perturbations identified the lateral motor-related superior colliculus (lSCm) as a key node controlling distractor engagement. Retinal inputs to the sensory-related SC signalled distractors even when mice ignored them. Pre-distractor behaviour and motor cortical activity predicted subsequent engagement, while increased corticocollicular and decreased nigrocollicular activity before distractor onset were consistent with a permissive state for override. Suppressing corticocollicular transmission weakened override without detectably altering task engagement. Single-unit recordings in head-fixed mice revealed response amplification in subsets of lSCm neurons during combined retinal and motor cortical stimulation, despite weak responses to either input alone. Motor cortical input thus facilitates sensory recruitment of collicular action circuits, shaping the balance between action stability and action override during ongoing goal pursuit.
